title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks (Comprehensive)
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Overview

This document is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference's serving runtime. It consolidates the runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling/playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and the team wiki pointers. Intended audience: serving-runtime engineers, SREs, applied ML engineers onboarding new models, and release engineers.

Key goals:
- Maintain consistent low-latency, high-throughput inference across hosted, dedicated and private deployments.
- Provide reproducible profiling and benchmarking artifacts.
- Codify operational runbooks for common incidents and upgrades.

Scope and conventions
- Component names reflect service names in prod (runtime-agent, inference-router, batch-coordinator, kv-cache, kernel-manager).
- All numeric thresholds are SLO targets unless marked as capacity limits or emergency thresholds.

1) Runtime architecture (overview)

Summary:
The runtime is comprised of a lightweight control plane (orchestrator) and a GPU-optimized serving plane. The orchestrator handles request routing, model variant selection, rollout policies, and autoscaling signals. The serving plane hosts per-GPU workers that run the inference kernels, manage KV caches, and expose a local gRPC endpoint to the orchestrator.

Primary components:
- inference-router: front-line gateway that implements routing policies (latency-based, cost-based, region-aware).
- runtime-agent: per-node process that manages worker lifecycle, local caches, and telemetry.
- kernel-manager: selects optimized kernels and execution paths (FP16, int8/4 quantized kernels, fused attention) per model and per request shape.
- batch-coordinator: continuous-batching manager that decides batch cutoffs to balance latency and throughput.
- kv-cache: sharded parameter/activation prefix cache with async persistence for warm-starting recurrent sessions.
- telemetry-collector: aggregates token-level latencies, GPU utilization, and batching statistics.

Sequence of request flow:
1. Client -> inference-router (auth, quotas, basic validation).
2. Router consults model-catalog & routing policy; selects target pool or variant and forwards to runtime-agent.
3. runtime-agent examines KV cache, decides cache-hit vs cold-path.
4. batch-coordinator aggregates requests into a batch (bounded by max_batch_size and max_wait_ms).
5. kernel-manager selects kernel path; dispatch to GPU worker.
6. GPU worker executes and updates KV-cache and tracing.
7. Response streamed back to client; telemetry emitted.

SLOs and capacities (summary):
- Short-query SLO (<=128 tokens): p50 < 12ms, p95 < 65ms (single-token-generation step), availability 99.95%.
- Medium query SLO (128-1024 tokens): p50 < 45ms, p95 < 220ms.
- Throughput target: per-GPU steady-state 5000 tokens/sec (NVIDIA H100, bf16, optimized kernels).
- Max_batch_size default: 128 sequences; max_wait_ms default: 12 ms. Adjust with workload profile.

2) Kernel scheduling design and rationale

Goals:
- Minimize end-to-end latency while maintaining GPU utilization.
- Automatically adapt kernel selection to model architecture, sequence length, and hardware.

Design highlights:
- Multi-tier scheduling: immediate (low-latency) queue for latency-sensitive requests and opportunistic (throughput) queue for batchable non-latency-sensitive requests.
- Kernel fingerprinting: each model variant has a precomputed fingerprint (model size, head size, layer count, quantization profile) used by kernel-manager to map to a kernel binary and parameterization.
- Adaptive cutover: if queue depth exceeds threshold or p95 latency drifts past threshold, runtime shifts to pre-warmed quantized kernels or lower-precision kernels with monitored quality regression flags.
- Preemption policy: small batches (<=4 sequences) from latency queue preempt large throughput batches if waiting time would exceed latency SLO.

Config knobs (tunable per-deployment):
- max_wait_ms (int): max time to hold batch before dispatch. Default: 12
- max_batch_size (int): upper bound sequences per batch. Default: 128
- latency_queue_capacity (int): concurrent small batches reserved per GPU. Default: 16
- adaptive_cutover_enabled (bool): toggle for automatic precision fallback. Default: true

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile a model / workload)

Purpose: Provide a repeatable procedure for diagnosing latency regressions and finding kernel-level hotspots.

Step-by-step profiling procedure:
1. Reproduce load shape: use load-generator with representative prompt lengths and concurrency. Example CLI:

```bash
# example using rdinfer-loadgen (internal)
rdinfer-loadgen --model my-model:2026-01 --qps 200 --prompt-set ./prompts/ssr.json --concurrency 64 --duration 5m --streaming=false
```

2. Collect system-level telemetry for the profiling window:
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,temperature.gpu --format=csv -l 1
- /opt/redwood/bin/runtime-metrics dump --window 5m --out /tmp/metrics.json

3. Enable kernel-level tracing: set KERNEL_TRACE=1 in runtime-agent and reproduce short synthetic batch. This produces kernel_trace.pb.

4. Post-process traces with trace-analyzer:
```bash
trace-analyzer kernel_trace.pb --output /tmp/trace-report.html
```
Look for: frequent kernel launches (<1ms) causing CPU-GPU synchronization, large memcpy costs, or suboptimal kernel selection for typical sequence lengths.

5. Hypothesis and experiment:
- If memcpy dominates: enable pinned-memory path (RUNTIME_PINNED_MEM=true) and re-profile.
- If kernel launch overhead dominates for small sequences: reduce kernel granularity or enable fused attention kernels for that model size.
- If batching behavior causes tail latency: reduce max_wait_ms or provide per-route latency-priority override.

6. Quality checks: for quantization fallback experiments, run the model QA harness and compare evaluation suites (approx. 500 prompt/eval pairs). Threshold: model quality drops no more than 1.5% relative to baseline for controlled rollouts.

4) Benchmarking suite (reproducible benchmarks and how to run them)

Bench framework components:
- benchmark-scenarios: JSON definitions of workload shapes (short-chat, long-form, batch-embedding, streaming-chat).
- harness: rdinfer-bench harness that orchestrates run, collates token-level latencies, GPU metrics, and cost estimates.
- golden-metrics: reference results for curated models and hardware (H100, A100, RTX6000).

How to run a standard benchmark:
1. Check out the repo and install the harness.
2. Run a canonical scenario: 
```bash
rdinfer-bench run --scenario short-chat --model my-model:2026-01 --hardware h100 --duration 10m --out results/short-chat-mymodel.json
```
3. Validate result by comparing to golden metrics:
```bash
bench-compare results/short-chat-mymodel.json golden/short-chat-h100.json --report /tmp/compare-report.html
```
Benchmark output fields (always produced):
- scenario (string)
- model (string)
- hardware (string)
- tokens_per_second (numeric string)
- p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms (numeric strings)
- avg_gpu_util_pct (numeric string)
- cost_estimate_per_million_tokens_usd (numeric string)

Bench best practices:
- Use isolated GPU nodes to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Run at multiple scales to surface nonlinear behavior on large batches.
- Commit scenario JSON and results as artifacts for release reviews.

5) Release notes (recent runtime releases)

v2026-02 (2026-02-15) - Major
- Kernel-manager: added fused-attention kernels for transformer layers with head_dim <= 64; expected 1.8x perf on short sequences.
- Batch-coordinator: improved adaptive batching algorithm to reduce p95 by 12% for mixed workloads.
- New telemetry: token-level cost tracking exported to observability pipeline.
- Migration: default max_wait_ms reduced 12 -> 10ms for hosted to improve tail latency.

v2026-01 (2025-11-30) - Minor
- KV-cache: fixed memory leak on cold-path population.
- Runtime-agent: improved graceful shutdown to reduce in-flight disruption during canary rollouts.
- Added new benchmark scenarios for streaming-chat.

Upgrade guidance:
1. Run the benchmark suite on a staging pool (tag: runtime-staging).
2. Deploy canary with 5% traffic and monitor: p95 latency, error rate, GPU OOMs for 30m.
3. If regressions observed, roll back canary and open an incident with the runtime-oncall page.

6) Known issues (active)

- Issue: Occasional p99 spikes when concurrent live sessions > 12k on A100 clusters (tracked: RUNTIME-5678). Workaround: scale out runtime-pool or enable adaptive_cutover. Owner: eng-serving-runtime. ETA fix: 2026-Q2.
- Issue: Streaming responses may sometimes reorder tokens for models with dynamic-length positional embeddings (RUNTIME-5521). Workaround: enable strict-positional-mode in model-variant config. Owner: applied-ml.
- Issue: Rare kernel crash during quantized int4 path for 30B models on older driver versions (RUNTIME-5409). Workaround: pin driver >=535.x or fallback to int8. Owner: kernel-team.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook: High p95 latency on hosted API
1. Verify alert and scope: check per-route p95 dashboards and correlate with model, region, and pool.
2. Isolate impacted pool: use runtime-admin list-pools --filter p95>150ms
3. Check queue depths: runtime-metrics top-queues --pool <pool-id>
4. If latency due to batching tail: temporarily reduce max_batch_size by 25% and max_wait_ms by 50% for the route.
5. If due to GPU saturation: scale out pool by +20% capacity or redirect traffic to a compatible lower-cost model variant.
6. If due to kernel crashes: check /var/log/runtime/kernel-errors.log and escalate to kernel-team.
7. Post-incident: run profiling playbook and update runbook with root cause.

Runbook: GPU OOM errors during rollout
1. Pause rollout.
2. Inspect model config for unexpected kv-cache sizing or sequence-length defaults.
3. Run local reproduce with rdinfer-loadgen at 2x canary traffic.
4. If OOM confirmed: reduce per-worker concurrency or enable quantization-profile fallback.
5. Once fixed, roll canary to 10% and continue monitoring.

8) Team wiki & ownership

Primary owning team: eng-serving-runtime (pager: #runtime-oncall). Secondary owners: kernel-team, applied-ml, eng-sre.

Useful pages and artifacts:
- serving-runtime-runbooks-and-playbook-2026.json (runbooks and quick remediations)
- serving-runtime-architecture-and-profiling-playbook-2026.json (deep-dive profiling)
- kernel-and-scheduling/internal-kernel-fingerprints.csv (artifact in s3)
- benchmarks/golden-metrics/ (CI artifact store)

Onboarding checklist for new joiners:
1. Read this page and serving-runtime-architecture deep-dive.
2. Run the micro-benchmark scenario on a dev H100 node.
3. Shadow an oncall rotation and run through the high-p95 playbook.
4. Complete the kernel-fingerprint lab and submit PR for a small model.

9) References & appendix

Appendix A - Useful CLI snippets:
- Dump runtime metrics for last 10 minutes:
```bash
/opt/redwood/bin/runtime-metrics dump --window 10m --out /tmp/metrics.json
```
- Trigger canary with 5% traffic:
```bash
runtime-admin rollout --model my-model:2026-02 --pool prod-east --canary 5
```
Appendix B - Common configuration table (editable per-deployment)

| key | description | default | notes |
|-----|-------------|---------|-------|
| max_wait_ms | Max time to hold batches before dispatch | 12 ms | Lower for latency-sensitive routes |
| max_batch_size | Max sequences per batch | 128 | Tune by model size and GPU memory |
| adaptive_cutover_enabled | Fallback to lower precision kernels | true | Watch eval-quality regression |

Appendix C - Incident contacts:
- eng-serving-runtime oncall: #runtime-oncall (PagerDuty)
- kernel-team lead: kernel-lead@redwood.example.com
- applied-ml triage: applied-ml@redwood.example.com

Document maintenance
- Owner: Ava Martinez (eng-serving-runtime)
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major release.
- How to propose edits: open PR against confluence markdown repo with CHANGELOG entry and request reviewers: Marcus Liu, Priya Desai.
